title: The new martyrs of Russia
hookLine: after the Russian Revolution, priests, nuns and lay people are killed or sent to camps

lines: A NUN WHO NURSES THE POOR.
cards: Before the revolution, she was a princess. Elizabeth, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria, married into the Russian royal family.
When a bomb killed her husband, she went to the prison, visited the man who had thrown it, and told him she forgave him.
Then she gave away her jewels, put on a plain religious habit, and opened a convent in Moscow to nurse the poor. After the revolution, she was arrested.
Tradition says that when her captors threw her and others down a mine shaft, people heard them singing hymns from below.

teach.b: After the Russian Revolution, the new Soviet state set out to push religion out of public life. Churches were closed, looted, turned into warehouses or blown up.
Bishops, priests, monks and nuns were shot or sent to labor camps in the far north and east. So were ordinary parishioners: a church warden, a choir singer, a grandmother who hid icons.
On the island of Solovki, an old monastery became a prison camp.
The Orthodox Church calls these people the new martyrs and confessors of Russia. A martyr dies for the faith; a confessor suffers for it and lives. Now the word inside the word.
Before Jesus rises into heaven, he tells his followers, in the King James Bible: "ye shall be witnesses unto me."
Later the Greek word behind witness is put into English another way, in Revelation: "Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you." Witness and martyr, one word.
A martyr is first a witness. What did these witnesses do?
Accounts from the camps describe priests hearing confessions in whispers during work, Easter hymns sung under the breath in a barracks, bread saved to share with someone weaker.
Faithfulness in small hidden ways, where it could cost everything. Revelation has a line written to a suffering church: "be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life."
The same years were hard for Catholics, Baptists, Jews, Muslims and Buddhists under that state too. The Orthodox Church now keeps a feast for its new martyrs, and reads their names.

how: The Russian Orthodox Church keeps a feast of the new martyrs and confessors of Russia, with icons that gather many of them together, and parishes pray for those who suffer for their faith.

o: Greek for one who suffers for the faith and lives
Greek for witness, the root of our word martyr

witnesses in Acts 1:8, and my faithful martyr in Revelation 2:13.

games.q: you're a priest in a labor camp. it's Easter, and worship is forbidden. what do you do?
o: do nothing. it isn't worth the risk.
hold a loud service in the yard.
sing the Easter hymn under your breath with whoever is near.
games.why: accounts from the camps describe Easter hymns sung under the breath in the barracks: faithfulness in small hidden ways.

practice: People are still punished today, in different places and under different powers, for what they believe or how they worship: some Christians, some of other faiths or none.
Picture one person in a cell tonight because of what they believe; you don't need their name. If you pray, ask that they be kept faithful and safe; if not, let them be real to you for a while.

wordCard.voice: martys. Greek for witness, the word behind martyr, the Orthodox Christians who were killed or sent to camps under Soviet rule and are honored as witnesses.

orig.note: Greek: a witness; in Acts 1:8 the King James Bible says witnesses, in Revelation 2:13 martyr.

carryVoice: Your line: faithful in the camps. Small, hidden, and faithful anyway. That's day nine hundred forty-four.
